title: Net Billing Calculator Pakistan 2026 (Old vs New) | Wattlyst
meta: Compare your bill under old net metering and the 2026 net billing rules. Enter units imported and exported; see the bill and the export credit in PKR.
author: ali-ahmad

sections.h2: Net metering calculator vs net billing: what changed in 2026?
p: Under the old net metering rules a bidirectional meter counted units in and units out, and the DISCO billed only the difference. Every exported unit cancelled an imported unit at the same slab rate, and if you exported more than you imported the spare units carried forward to the next month.

Under the NEPRA Prosumer Regulations notified in 2026, new solar connections are on net billing. Imports are billed at the normal slab rate of the band your imported units reach, and exports are bought at a flat buyback rate that is far below the slab rate. The two numbers are worked out separately and then set against each other, which is why the same month costs more under net billing.

Agreements signed before 9 February 2026 keep the rate and rules of the old net-metering regulations until they expire, unless the system is enlarged, which moves it to net billing; renewals move to net billing. Ask your DISCO when your agreement ends.

sections.h2: How is a net metering bill calculated in Pakistan?
p: Old rules: net units = imported − exported. If the result is positive, those net units are billed at the slab they reach, exactly like a home without solar. If the result is negative, the bill for energy is zero and the spare units are credited to the next month. For the default month above that gives 100 net units at Rs 22.44 = Rs 2,244.

New rules (net billing): imported units × slab rate gives the import bill, Rs 14,584 for 400 units here. Exported units × buyback rate gives the credit, Rs 2,439 for 300 units. Bill = import bill − credit = Rs 12,145. Because all imported units are charged at the slab their total reaches, exporting does not pull you into a lower slab any more.

sections.h2: What is the net billing rate for solar exports in Pakistan?
p: The calculator uses Rs 8.13 per exported unit. The NEPRA (Prosumer) Regulations 2026, notified 9 Feb 2026, credit exported units at the national average energy purchase price, and NEPRA's power purchase price decision for CY 2026 puts that price at Rs 8.13. NEPRA sets it again for each year and may revise it by notification, so change the buyback field if your bill shows a different rate.

Compare that with the import rate of Rs 36.46 per unit for 400 units: a unit you export is worth a fraction of a unit you import. Using your own solar power in the day, running the water pump, washing machine and AC while the sun is up, is worth more than exporting it; check how much your panels will make tomorrow to plan those loads for the sunniest hours.

sections.h2: Does excess export still carry forward?
p: Yes, in rupees rather than units. If the export credit for the month is larger than the import bill, the bill for energy is zero and the spare credit carries forward to the next month. The calculator shows the carry-forward amount instead of a negative bill. Under old net metering it was spare units that carried forward.

faq.q: What is the net billing calculation for a solar home?
faq.a: Imported units × the slab rate they reach, minus exported units × the buyback rate. For 400 imported and 300 exported units that is Rs 14,584 − Rs 2,439 = Rs 12,145 in energy charges.

faq.q: What is the solar export rate in Pakistan?
faq.a: Rs 8.13 per unit for CY 2026: the national average energy purchase price in NEPRA's power purchase price decision, which the NEPRA (Prosumer) Regulations 2026, notified 9 Feb 2026, use for exported units. Under old net metering exported units first cancelled imported ones unit for unit.

faq.q: Why do some sites say Rs 11 a unit for exported solar units?
faq.a: News reports in February 2026 quoted a buyback of about Rs 11 a unit that was under discussion; NEPRA did not notify it (Express Tribune report in Sources), and some sites still quote it. NEPRA's power purchase price decision for CY 2026 sets the national average energy purchase price at Rs 8.13, and that is the rate the Prosumer Regulations use for exported units. If your agreement or DISCO credits a different rate, type it in the buyback box and compare both results.

faq.q: How much does a solar home save under net metering compared with net billing?
faq.a: For the default month, old net metering charged Rs 2,244 and net billing charges Rs 12,145, so net metering saved Rs 9,901 more. Savings against having no solar at all are larger under both, because every unit you use in the day is not bought at all.

faq.q: Is there a solar payback calculator for Pakistan?
faq.a: Yes, on this page. Enter your monthly units before solar and the system price: the saving is the energy charge of those units without solar minus the net billing charge, and payback in years is the price divided by twelve months of that saving. A home that used 600 units a month before solar and now imports 400 and exports 300 saves Rs 11,987 a month, so a Rs 600,000 system pays back in 4.2 years. The saving counts energy charges only; GST and the other per-unit lines on the units you no longer buy make the real payback shorter.

faq.q: Does the buyback rate for solar change?
faq.a: Yes. It is the national average energy purchase price, which NEPRA sets for each year and may revise by notification. If your bill shows a different rate, enter it in the buyback field.

faq.q: How are net metering units calculated on the bill?
faq.a: The bidirectional meter has an import reading and an export reading. Under old net metering the DISCO billed import minus export; under net billing the two readings are priced separately and set against each other in rupees. This calculator accepts both readings and shows both results.

faq.q: Can I still apply for net metering in 2026?
faq.a: New connections under the Prosumer Regulations are on net billing. Agreements signed before 9 February 2026 keep the rate and rules of the old net-metering regulations until they expire, unless the system is enlarged, which moves it to net billing; renewals move to net billing.

key_facts: Under net billing the imported units are billed at the normal slab rate (Rs 36.46 per unit for 400 units) and exported units are bought back at a flat rate, Rs 8.13 per unit, NEPRA's national average energy purchase price for CY 2026.
Under old net metering exported units cancelled imported units one for one, so a home importing 400 and exporting 300 units paid for only 100 units, at the lower slab those units reach (Rs 22.44).
For the same 400 imported and 300 exported units, net billing charges Rs 12,145 and old net metering Rs 2,244: a difference of Rs 9,901 a month in energy charges alone.
The net billing figure is energy charges only; the fixed charge per sanctioned kW, FC surcharge, QTA, FPA and GST are added on the real bill.
mistakes: Subtracting exports from imports first. Under net billing all imported units are billed at the slab their total reaches; only the rupee credit is subtracted afterwards.
Treating this as the full bill. The result is the energy charge only; the fixed charge, FC surcharge, QTA, FPA and GST come on top and are worked out by the bill calculator.
Using the buyback rate as a fixed fact. It is an estimate until NEPRA or your DISCO publishes it; enter the rate from your own bill.
Ticking protected when a single month in the last six went over the limit. One high month moves you to unprotected rates for every unit.

fields.hint: Tick only if every one of your last six bills was within the protected unit limit. Not at 5 kW or more.

fields.label: Units a month before solar
fields.hint: For the saving and the payback: the units of an average month before you had solar (a year's units divided by twelve is best). It cannot be less than the units you import now.

legal.t: This is an estimate, not an official bill. Your DISCO's bill and NEPRA's tariff notifications are the official figures. Do not use this result as evidence before a court, NEPRA, the Wafaqi Mohtasib or any other forum. To dispute a bill, complain to your DISCO first, using the complaint number printed on your bill, then file a NEPRA complaint or a Wafaqi Mohtasib complaint.

examples.title: Import 400 units, export 300 units, and the payback
examples.text: Import bill 400 × Rs 36.46 (301–400 units slab) = Rs 14,584; export credit 300 × Rs 8.13 = Rs 2,439; net billing charge Rs 12,145. Old net metering billed 100 net units at Rs 22.44 = Rs 2,244, so net billing costs Rs 9,901 more. Before solar the home used 600 units, an energy charge of Rs 24,132; net billing saves Rs 11,987 a month, Rs 143,844 a year, so a Rs 600,000 system pays back in 4.2 years on energy charges alone, before any change in tariff or panel output.

examples.title: Export more than you import: 200 in, 500 out
examples.text: Import bill Rs 5,782 at Rs 28.91 a unit (101–200 units slab); export credit Rs 4,065. Net billing still leaves Rs 1,717 to pay, because the credit per exported unit is lower than the cost per imported unit. Under old net metering the energy bill was Rs 0 and 300 units carried forward.

examples.title: Credit larger than the import bill: 100 in, 300 out
examples.text: Import bill 100 × Rs 22.44 (1–100 units slab) = Rs 2,244; export credit Rs 2,439. The energy charge is Rs 0 and Rs 195 of credit carries forward to next month. Under old net metering 200 spare units would have carried forward instead.

examples.title: Protected consumer: 150 in, 100 out
examples.text: A protected home is billed slab-wise at the protected rates up to Rs 13.01 in the 101–200 units protected slab, so the import bill is Rs 1,705. The export credit is Rs 813 and the net billing charge Rs 892, against Rs 527 for 50 net units under old net metering: Rs 365 more. The gap is small because protected rates are close to the buyback rate.

examples.title: ToU meter, 8 kW: 500 in (150 in peak hours), 300 out
examples.text: At 5 kW or more the import is billed on peak and off-peak rates: 150 peak units × Rs 46.85 + 350 off-peak × Rs 34.53 = Rs 19,113; export credit Rs 2,439; net billing charge Rs 16,674. Solar exports happen in daylight, which is off-peak, so old net metering netted them against the off-peak import only: 150 peak units × Rs 46.85 + 50 off-peak units left after the export × Rs 34.53 = Rs 8,754. Net billing costs Rs 7,920 more. Without the peak units from your bill, the tool assumes 25% of the import falls in peak hours, an estimate.

content.answer: A home that imports 400 units and exports 300 units pays about Rs 12,145 in energy charges under net billing, against Rs 2,244 under old net metering, so net billing costs Rs 9,901 more that month. Net bill = imported units × slab rate − exported units × buyback rate of Rs 8.13.

formula.text: Net billing Rs = max(0, import × slab rate − export × buyback); old net metering Rs = max(0, import − export) × slab rate of the net units
lines: import = units taken from the grid in the month
export = units sent to the grid in the month
slab rate = unprotected (or protected) A-1 rate of the band the units reach
buyback = flat Rs per exported unit under net billing
Credit larger than the import bill carries forward to the next month
Extra = net billing Rs − old net metering Rs, never below zero

content.safety: Only a AEDB-certified installer and a licensed electrician may connect a solar system for export, and the bidirectional meter is installed by the DISCO; never bypass the meter or back-feed the grid through a plug socket.
